summary: Alaska requires every contractor, including specialty installers, to hold a state contractor registration (with bond and insurance) before bidding or working. Lavatory partitions fall under the sheet metal specialty category.
authority: Alaska Division of Corporations, Business and Professional Licensing (Construction Contractors)
note: AS 08.18.011 requires registration to bid or work, no dollar threshold seen. 12 AAC 21.480 sheet metal specialty lists 'lavatory partitions'. Specialty bond $10,000 (AS 08.18.101/.171 area). Exemption 08.18.161(5) covers products that do not become a permanent fixed part of a structure; fixed partitions likely not covered. Plus Alaska business license and workers comp. Registration functions as the state license.

summary: Commercial jobs of $100,000 or more need a state license from the Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors. Smaller partition installs generally don't need a state license, but cities and counties may require their own business registration.
authority: Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors
note: Board page confirms threshold raised $50k to $100k effective 2024-10-01 (Act 2024-277). Many third-party guides still say $50k. Act 2026-396 (eff. 2026-10-01) amended 34-8-7 with new exemptions (routine maintenance, pools); thresholds not visible, full act PDF not read. Subcontractor treatment (sub of a licensed GC) not verified. No specialty class for partitions found. Confirm with board.

summary: Commercial jobs of $50,000 or more (labor and materials) need a license from the Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board; the board has a specialty class that includes partitions. Smaller jobs don't need a state license, and splitting a job to stay under is barred.
authority: Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board
note: ACA 17-25-103: commercial contractor = non-residential work $50,000 or more; anti-splitting clause. Rule 17 CAR 255-308 specialty list includes 'Furniture, recreational and/or playground equipment, bleachers, seating, and partitions' (specialty minimum net worth $5,000). Building permit offices must see license at $50k+.

summary: Arizona requires a state Registrar of Contractors license for commercial installation work of $1,000 or more. Smaller casual jobs without a permit are exempt, but a commercial partition installer should plan on being licensed.
authority: Arizona Registrar of Contractors
note: ARS 32-1121(A)(14): exempt only if aggregate price under $1,000, casual/minor, no permit, no advertising as contractor. Exact classification for toilet partitions NOT confirmed: R4-9-102 text (Cornell copy) shows C-10 Drywall (movable partitions, nonbearing steel partitions), C-24 Ornamental Metals, C-27 (closed to new applicants); no 'toilet partition' wording. Ask ROC which C/CR class applies (a CR-10 style dual or B-general may be used).

summary: California requires a CSLB license, usually the C-61/D-34 Prefabricated Equipment classification, for partition installs of $1,000 or more. Jobs needing workers or permits require a license at any price.
authority: California Contractors State License Board (CSLB)
note: D-34 page text: 'all forms and types of toilet/shower room partitions/accessories'. Threshold: CSLB press release #24-21 (cslb.ca.gov/Resources/PressReleases/2024/AB2622.FINAL.pdf) and #24-07: AB 2622 (Ch. 240, Stats 2024) raised minor-work exemption $500 to $1,000 effective 2025-01-01, only if no workers hired and no permit. B (General Building) can also do it. Public school work (DSA) usually requires license regardless.

summary: Colorado doesn't license general or specialty contractors at the state level; only trades like electrical and plumbing are state licensed. Cities and counties set their own contractor licensing and registration rules.
authority: Colorado Department of Regulatory Agencies (DORA); local city and county building departments
note: DORA consumer page (seen via search result snippet; direct fetch blocked 403) says not all occupations are licensed, e.g. roofers and general contractors. Local licensing varies (Denver etc.); not researched per-city. Electrical/plumbing state licenses not relevant to partitions.

summary: Connecticut doesn't require a state contractor license to install toilet partitions in typical commercial buildings. A Major Contractor registration applies only to large structural work on very large buildings. Check local requirements.
authority: Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection
note: Major Contractor Registration (CGS ch. 541) applies to threshold buildings (4 stories, 60 ft, 150 ft span, 150,000 sq ft, 1,000 occupancy) and structural integrity work; partitions are non-structural. Home Improvement Contractor registration applies to residential only. Trade licenses (electrical, plumbing etc.) separate. Confirm with DCP for large/institutional buildings.

summary: DC licenses general contractors and construction managers through the Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection. Whether a partition installer working as a subcontractor needs that license isn't clear, so confirm with DLCP.
authority: DC Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (DLCP)
note: DLCP page only confirms General Contractor/Construction Manager is a licensed category (with Basic Business License + insurance COI). Secondary sources say GC/CM license is tiered by contract size (Class A-E) and some say no commercial GC license exists; Law 25-244 may split commercial/residential licensing. Need DLCP answer on subcontract specialty installers. Could not open DCMR text.

summary: Delaware has no state contractor license, but contractors doing construction work, including commercial, must register with the Department of Labor's Contractor Registration program and hold a state business license. Local rules may add requirements.
authority: Delaware Department of Labor, Office of Contractor Registration
note: 19 Del. C. ch. 36: 'construction services' includes all building or work on a building, structure or improvement; no general exemption list in 3602/3603. Registration fee about $200/yr (per secondary sources, $300 with state contract). Out-of-state firms need nonresident registration and bond (secondary source). Material suppliers excluded from 'worker' only. Also Delaware business license from Division of Revenue.

summary: Florida has no state license category specifically for toilet partitions, and local governments can't require a license for work outside the state's defined categories. Contractors whose work matches a licensed category do need one; confirm with the state board.
authority: Florida Construction Industry Licensing Board (DBPR)
note: Fla. Stat. 489.103(9) exempts work under $2,500 casual/minor. 489.105(3) defines categories; partitions not named; specialty categories set by board rule (61G4-15), none for partitions found. 489.113(6)/163.211 (HB 735 2021, HB 1383 ch. 2023-271) bar local licensing outside matching scopes. Risk: a county may view interior build-out as general/building contractor scope. Not verified with DBPR. Statute pages opened: 489.103, 489.105, 489.113.

summary: Georgia requires a state license for general contracting work over $2,500, but limited specialty trade work may be exempt. Whether a partition installer needs a license depends on how the job is contracted, so confirm with the state board.
authority: Georgia State Licensing Board for Residential and General Contractors
note: Official pages returned 403, so only search snippets seen. O.C.G.A. 43-41-2: $2,500 (work value or compensation, whichever higher). A secondary source says 43-41-17(f) exempts specialty/limited/specific-trade contractors, but unverified; text could mean work for a licensed GC only. Commercial general contractor license for building construction; electrical/plumbing/conditioned air separate under ch. 14. Need confirmation from board. One site claims $100k commercial threshold - unsupported.

summary: Hawaii requires a state contractor license for most work above about $1,500, and the C-25 Institutional and Commercial Equipment specialty covers stationary metal partitions. Confirm the current limit with the Contractors License Board.
authority: Hawaii Contractors License Board (DCCA)
note: Classification PDF: C-25 includes 'folding and sliding partitions... stationary metal partitions' and lockers; C-5 covers nonbearing partitions; C-44 sheet metal covers nonbearing metal partitions. Threshold: HRS 444-2 handyman exemption raised from $1,000 to $1,500 by Act 283 (2019) per text of 2026 bill HB846 (not enacted as far as seen; proposed $2,500). HRS page itself returned 403 - verify. Applies to labor, materials plus other conditions; commercial work generally licensed.

summary: Iowa requires construction contractors, including subcontractors, who earn $2,000 or more a year from construction to register with the state each year. It is a registration (not a skills license) and requires an Iowa unemployment insurance number.
authority: Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals, and Licensing (DIAL)
note: Verified on DIAL page and Iowa Code 91C.1. Program moved from Iowa Workforce Development to DIAL. $50 fee, annual renewal; out-of-state contractors generally need a $25,000 bond; employers need workers comp certificate. Plumbing/mechanical need separate license.

summary: Idaho requires contractors to register with the state for jobs over $2,000. Publicly funded jobs of $50,000 or more, such as school projects, need a separate Public Works Contractor license.
authority: Idaho Division of Occupational and Professional Licenses (Idaho Contractors Board)
note: DOPL FAQ: registration for construction job exceeding $2,000 (materials and labor); commercial owners maintaining own buildings exempt. Idaho Code 54-5205(2)(f). Public Works license threshold $50,000 (Idaho Code 54-1901 et seq.) comes from search snippets, not opened in the official statute. Registration is for private work; electrical/plumbing/HVAC separately licensed.

summary: Illinois has no state license for general or specialty interior contractors such as partition installers. Some cities license contractors themselves, for example Chicago requires its own general contractor license, so check the city where the restroom is.
authority: Illinois Dept. of Financial and Professional Regulation (state); local building department / City of Chicago Dept. of Buildings
note: IDFPR home page opened but did not itself state the absence of a GC license; conclusion rests on secondary guides (state licenses roofing via IDFPR, plumbing via IDPH; Chicago licenses GCs at city level). Confirm Chicago's GC/trade rules for partition work and IDFPR licensed-professions list (idfpr.illinois.gov/profs/proflist.html).

summary: Indiana does not license general or specialty contractors at state level for work like partition installation. The state licenses trades such as plumbing; cities and counties may have their own contractor registration, so check locally.
authority: Indiana Professional Licensing Agency; local building department
note: PLA professions list shows no general/specialty contractor category (only plumbing and manufactured home installers among construction trades). Electrical and HVAC are locally licensed in Indiana (not verified here). Some cities (e.g., Indianapolis) register contractors; not checked.

summary: Kansas has no state license for general or specialty interior contractors such as partition installers. Licensing and registration happen at city or county level, so installers should check the local building department.
authority: Local city/county building department (state: Kansas Secretary of State business registration only)
note: Official Kansas pages returned 403; conclusion based on secondary guides. State-level exception is roofing registration (Kansas Attorney General). Confirm with a city (e.g., Wichita, Overland Park, Johnson County) before publishing; no official URL opened.

summary: Kentucky does not license general contractors at state level for work like partition installation. The state licenses electricians, plumbers, boiler and fire protection contractors; some cities and counties require their own contractor licenses.
authority: Kentucky Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction; local city/county licensing
note: DHBC page lists licensed trades (plumbers, electricians, boiler, sprinkler/fire alarm) with no general or specialty contractor license; page silent on GC licensing. HVAC licensing is state-level in KY per other sources (not confirmed here). Local licenses (e.g., Louisville, Lexington) not checked.

summary: Louisiana requires a state commercial contractor license for commercial projects of $50,000 or more including labor and materials, and for subcontractors on such jobs. Smaller jobs fall below the state requirement; local rules may still apply.
authority: Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors (LSLBC)
note: Threshold verified on LSLBC Types of Licenses page (effective Aug 2024). Electrical/mechanical/plumbing threshold is $10,000. Exams/Classifications page has S.7 'Glass, Glazing, Store Fronts, Metal Partitions, Panels and Siding' (trade exam) as closest fit, and S 'Limited Specialty Services' (no exam) for work over $50,000 not covered elsewhere; toilet partitions not named. Confirm classification with the board.

summary: Massachusetts home improvement registration applies to residential work. Commercial interior work such as partitions has no state contractor license, though structural work may need a licensed construction supervisor and local building permits; check with the building department.
authority: Massachusetts Division of Occupational Licensure / Office of Public Safety and Inspections (construction supervisor licensing); local building department
note: mass.gov pages returned 403; not verified. Construction supervisor license (CSL) is tied to building permits for structural work under 780 CMR; unclear whether non-structural partition installs in commercial space need a CSL holder. Local permit requirements vary. Confirm with DOL/OPSI.

summary: Maryland's state home improvement license covers residential work only. For commercial work a construction license from the Clerk of the Circuit Court, or local county or city registration, may be needed, so installers should check where the job is.
authority: Maryland Department of Labor (Home Improvement Commission is residential only); Clerks of the Circuit Court / local jurisdiction
note: Official Labor page says a Circuit Court clerk construction license 'may be necessary' for commercial or agricultural construction contracts, so this is a county-level license, not a state board license. Could argue 'unclear'; confirm exact applicability to partition installers with a Circuit Court clerk.

summary: Maine has no state license for general or specialty interior contractors such as partition installers. The state licenses trades like electricians and plumbers; towns handle building permits.
authority: Maine Dept. of Professional and Financial Regulation; local code enforcement office
note: Maine PFR pages returned 403; based on general knowledge and secondary guides (state licenses electricians, plumbers, oil/propane and similar trades, no GC license). No official URL opened; confirm with PFR.

summary: Michigan licenses residential builders and maintenance and alteration contractors, but has no state license for commercial interior work such as partition installation. Some cities require local registration, so check with the local building department.
authority: Michigan Dept. of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs (LARA); local building department
note: LARA pages returned 403; based on search results (residential license threshold $600; no commercial GC license). Mechanical, electrical, plumbing licensed separately. Some cities (Detroit, Grand Rapids) reportedly require local registration. Confirm on michigan.gov/lara.

summary: Minnesota requires contractors doing commercial construction work who do not hold a residential contractor license to register with the state Department of Labor and Industry. It is a registration, not a skills license, and needs a workers' compensation certificate.
authority: Minnesota Department of Labor and Industry (Construction Contractor Registration)
note: DLI page opened: registration covers 'all commercial projects' for those without a residential license; no dollar threshold stated, fee not stated. Exemptions (e.g., employees of registered business, specific license holders) not detailed on page. Confirm whether pure product-install subcontractors are covered.

summary: Missouri has no state license for general or specialty interior contractors such as partition installers. Some cities and counties, such as St. Louis and Kansas City, require their own contractor licenses or registration.
authority: Local city/county licensing office (state: Missouri Division of Professional Registration licenses only certain trades)
note: Missouri state pages returned 503; based on general knowledge that Missouri has no statewide GC/specialty contractor license. Search returned nothing on Missouri. Confirm with a local jurisdiction; no official URL opened.

summary: Mississippi requires a state contractor license for commercial jobs over $50,000. Bathroom partition installation is listed under the board's Limited Specialty Services classification, which needs no exam. Smaller jobs fall under the threshold; local rules may apply.
authority: Mississippi State Board of Contractors
note: Classifications page explicitly lists 'Installation of Construction Specialties, Furniture, and Equipment' (booths, closet systems, bathroom partitions) under Limited Specialty Services, $50,000 threshold. Main msboc.us page says commercial contractors must be licensed but gave no figure. Secondary sources conflict on some lower thresholds ($10,000 for MEP specialties). Confirm 'over' vs 'or more' $50,000 and any lower specialty thresholds with the board.

summary: Montana moved from contractor registration to a state construction contractor license on January 1, 2026. Installers offering construction work to others should hold a license from the Department of Labor and Industry; confirm exemptions, such as having no employees, with the Department.
authority: Montana Department of Labor & Industry, Construction Contractor License Program
note: DLI page confirms licensing replaced registration 1/1/2026 (HB 239; old MCA 39-9-201 repealed by Ch. 644, L. 2025). Exemptions live in MCA 37-45-104, not read. Old registration exempted contractors with no employees (independent contractor exemption); unclear if kept. No dollar threshold found. Confirm with DLI (406-444-6880).

summary: North Carolina requires a state general contractor license when the project is valued at $40,000 or more. Smaller partition jobs generally don't need one. Confirm with the Licensing Board for General Contractors.
authority: North Carolina Licensing Board for General Contractors
note: Official page: 'If a project is valued at $40,000 or more, your general contractor must have a license issued by the state.' Threshold raised from $30,000 on 2023-10-01 (G.S. 87-1) per secondary sources. Threshold is on the whole project cost, not just partition scope; board watches for split contracts. Local permit may still require proof of license or exemption.

summary: North Dakota requires a state contractor license for jobs over $4,000, with the license class set by contract size. A typical partition job above that amount needs a Secretary of State contractor license.
authority: North Dakota Secretary of State, Contractor Licensing
note: Official page: license required when job cost/value/price exceeds $4,000 (NDCC ch. 43-07); classes A (>$500k), B (up to $500k), C (up to $300k), D (up to $100k). Page lists no exemptions; call SOS (701-328-2900) for specialty-trade exemption questions. Fees are as the page lists them.

summary: Nebraska has no state contractor license. Installers doing work on other people's property must register with the Department of Labor, with workers' compensation proof if they have employees. Some cities and counties, such as Lincoln and Douglas County, add their own licenses.
authority: Nebraska Department of Labor, Contractor Registration (Labor Standards)
note: Official page: all contractors doing business in NE must register; annual fee rises to $40 on 2026-08-01 (was $25). No dollar threshold or exemptions listed on the page. Local licensing (Lincoln commercial business license, Douglas County exam/bond) came from secondary sources, not verified.

summary: New Hampshire has no state license for general or specialty construction contractors; the state licenses trades like electricians. Cities and towns may require local permits or registration, so check with the local building department.
authority: New Hampshire Office of Professional Licensure and Certification (OPLC)
note: No official page found that states 'no GC license' outright; conclusion rests on several third-party licensing guides plus OPLC electricians' board existing. That URL was only seen in search results, not opened. Confirm by phone with OPLC (603-271-2152). Partitions are not an electrical/plumbing trade.

summary: New Jersey has no state license for commercial installers. State home improvement contractor registration applies only to residential work. Commercial jobs fall under local rules, so check with the municipality where the restroom is located.
authority: New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs, Home Improvement Contractor Registration
note: Fetch of the FAQ page returned empty; conclusion (HIC Act under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136 ff. does not apply to commercial property) comes from search-result snippets of the Division's FAQ and municipal FAQs. Re-read FAQ for exact wording. Installers who also do residential work must register ($110 initial fee per NJBIA; bond/security added 2024). Some municipalities require local contractor registration.

summary: New Mexico requires a state contractor license for construction work. Partition installation is not named in the classification list, so installers typically hold a general building license (GB-98) or the miscellaneous specialty license (GS-29). Confirm which applies with the Construction Industries Division.
authority: New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department, Construction Industries Division (CID)
note: 14.6.6 NMAC read: toilet partitions not named; GS-29 is the catch-all for CID-regulated work not listed; GB-98 includes all GS scopes. GS-7 (drywall/non-structural stud) is nearest named scope. Statute (NMSA 60-13-1 ff.) bars acting as a contractor without a license; exemptions with dollar limits exist but were not read (some secondary sources say $7,200/year). Ask CID which class they assign for partition installs.

summary: Nevada requires a state contractor's license, and toilet partitions fall under the C-8 Glass and Glazing classification. Only small repair jobs under $1,000 that need no permit are exempt. Confirm the classification with the Nevada State Contractors Board.
authority: Nevada State Contractors Board
note: NAC 624.260 text read on the legislature site: C-8 may install, repair and replace enclosures for showers and tubs and toilet partitions; former C-8d holders deemed C-8 restricted to those enclosures/partitions. The $1,000 repair/maintenance exemption (NRS 624.220(6)) came from a search summary, not read in the statute; a $3,000+ partition job is above it anyway. Other classifications (e.g. general building B) may also cover it; confirm with NSCB.

summary: New York State does not license commercial installers like this. New York City requires general contractor registration with the Department of Buildings for certain work, and some counties license home improvement contractors. Check local rules for the building's location.
authority: NYC Department of Buildings (city); no statewide licensing agency
note: NYC page read says GC registration is tied to building 1-, 2-, 3-family homes (new building permits); it does not say whether interior commercial work needs it. Absence of a NYS general contractor license inferred from DOS licensing-services listing and secondary sources, not stated by an official page. HIC licensing is residential and local (NYC, Nassau, Suffolk, Westchester, Putnam, Rockland). Confirm NYC DOB for NYC jobs.

summary: Ohio licenses only five commercial trades at state level: electrical, HVAC, hydronics, plumbing and refrigeration. Partition installation isn't one of them, but many cities and counties have their own contractor registration, so check locally.
authority: Ohio Construction Industry Licensing Board (Ohio Department of Commerce)
note: The OCILB page was only seen in search results (my fetch of it returned 404), so the five-trade scope comes from the search summary of that page plus ORC ch. 4740. Local city/county contractor registration varies widely.

summary: Oklahoma has no state license for general construction or most specialty installers. The state licenses plumbing, electrical, mechanical and roofing work only. Cities and counties may have their own registration, so check locally.
authority: Oklahoma Construction Industries Board
note: CIB FAQ read: 'General Contractors are not currently required to have a state license in Oklahoma'; regulated trades are plumbing, electrical, mechanical, roofing, inspectors. Out-of-state contractors may need Oklahoma Tax Commission nonresident registration (secondary source, unverified). Local rules (OKC, Tulsa) apply.

summary: Oregon requires a Construction Contractors Board license with a commercial endorsement for commercial construction work, including specialty trades. Installers should hold a commercial specialty or general endorsement; confirm which level fits the job with the CCB.
authority: Oregon Construction Contractors Board (CCB)
note: CCB page read: license generally required for construction work on real property; commercial endorsements CGC1, CGC2, CSC1, CSC2 (commercial developer excluded) with bonds/insurance. No dollar threshold or exemption for partitions found. CSC1 vs CSC2 rules (project size limits) not confirmed on an official page (ORS 701.021 / OAR 812 not read). Ask CCB which level applies.

summary: Pennsylvania has no state license for commercial installers. State home improvement registration covers residential work only. Commercial jobs fall under local rules, such as Philadelphia's contractor license, so check with the municipality.
authority: Pennsylvania Office of Attorney General, Home Improvement Contractor Registration
note: HIC site returned 503 and AG instruction PDF 404, so not actually read; conclusion from search snippets (HICPA 73 P.S. 517.1 ff.: $5,000/yr residential threshold, commercial exempt) and Philadelphia code interpretation requiring local licenses for non-residential work. Confirm HICPA text. Retail-property subcontractor carve-out noted in AG instructions.

summary: Rhode Island requires contractors who build or repair commercial or residential structures to register with the state Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board. Commercial-only contractors are exempt from the pre-registration and continuing education courses.
authority: Rhode Island Contractors' Registration and Licensing Board (CRLB)
note: Rule text (Section 2.2) says every contractor, remodeler and most subcontractors must register; sub exclusions not stated on page. Minor work under $500 definition (2.4B) unclear re exemption. crb.ri.gov pages returned 403; search snippets of CRB FAQ say commercial contractors must be registered. Confirm whether a partition-only installer counts as a subcontractor needing registration.

summary: South Carolina requires a state contractor license when a commercial project's total construction cost is over $10,000. Smaller jobs fall below the state threshold; local business licenses may still apply.
authority: South Carolina Contractors' Licensing Board (LLR)
note: 2023 LLR update: threshold raised from $5,000 to >$10,000 for general and mechanical contracting (Act 69/H4115). Threshold is on total cost of construction, so a partition sub on a larger project may be pulled in. Specialty subclass 'Nonstructural Renovation' (formerly Interior Renovation) likely fits; not confirmed that partitions-only work needs it. Confirm with Board.

summary: South Dakota has no state contractor license for this work. Contractors do need a state contractor's tax license from the Department of Revenue. Check city or county rules where the job is.
authority: South Dakota Department of Revenue (contractor's excise tax); local city/county
note: DOR page confirms tax license is required for construction/installation work (tax, not competency, license). 'No state GC license' rests on secondary sources only; no official page opened stating it. Electrical/plumbing are state-licensed separately. Some cities license contractors.

summary: Tennessee requires a state contractor license to bid or take commercial projects of $25,000 or more. Subcontractors in trades like drywall or carpentry are not required to hold one when working for a contractor.
authority: Tennessee Board for Licensing Contractors
note: Board application package: license required for prime contracting >= $25,000; subs only for electrical, mechanical, plumbing, HVAC, roofing >= $25,000 and masonry >= $100,000; 'drywall, painting, landscaping, carpentry, etc.' subs exempt when working for a contractor. A partitions installer bidding directly to the owner/facility at $25k+ is a prime and needs a license (BC-B/commercial or a classification covering 60%). Under $25k: no state contractor license (home improvement license is residential).

summary: Texas does not license general or specialty contractors for this work at the state level. Cities may require contractor registration to pull permits, for example Dallas.
authority: Texas Governor's Office guide to state licenses; local city building departments
note: Official guide: 'General contractors are not required to obtain a license to practice in Texas.' Trade licenses (TDLR: electrical, ACR) do not cover partitions. Dallas Chapter 52 registration from prior notes not re-verified.

summary: Utah requires a contractor license for alteration or remodel work valued at $7,000 or more, including labor and materials. Between $3,000 and $7,000, a one-time insurance affirmation is filed with the state.
authority: Utah Division of Professional Licensing (DOPL)
note: Utah Code 58-55-305(1)(h) (version effective 5/7/2025; renumbering 1/1/2027): exempt if contracted value < $7,000 (affirmation required if > $3,000). Earlier $3,000 figure from secondary sources is outdated. Specialty classes are in R156-55a; no verified class for toilet partitions; (1)(i) exempts specialty classes not deemed significant to public health/safety. Ask DOPL which class, if any, covers partitions.

summary: Virginia requires a state contractor license for commercial jobs over $1,000. Class C covers single jobs up to $30,000, Class B up to $150,000, and Class A $150,000 and above.
authority: Virginia Board for Contractors (DPOR)
note: Va. Code 54.1-1100: Class C > $1,000 and < $30,000 per job (or < $250,000 per 12 months); Class B $30k-<$150k; Class A >= $150k. Class B/A also need net worth. Specialty designation for partitions not verified (DPOR has specialties e.g. CBC, drywall, ACM); confirm which designation. Exemptions in 54.1-1101 not read.

summary: Vermont has no state contractor license for commercial partition installation. State registration applies to residential contractors on jobs of $10,000 or more. Only electrical and plumbing work is state-licensed. Check town rules.
authority: Vermont Office of Professional Regulation (Secretary of State)
note: OPR FAQ: registration is for residential jobs >= $10,000 (since April 2023); not for commercial-only work. 'No general contractor license' for commercial relies on that plus secondary sources; no official statement opened saying so outright.

summary: Washington requires every construction contractor to register with Labor & Industries. Specialty contractors can only do work in their registered specialty and generally cannot hire subcontractors.
authority: Washington State Department of Labor & Industries (L&I)
note: Verified on L&I page: all construction contractors register; specialty only within specialty; $15,000 specialty bond vs $30,000 general. Registration (not exam-based licensing). Confirm which of the 63 specialties, if any, covers toilet partitions, or register as general.

summary: Wisconsin does not license contractors for commercial work at the state level. State licensing covers one- and two-family dwelling contractors and certain trades, such as electrical and HVAC. Commercial jobs go through state plan review and local permits.
authority: Wisconsin Department of Safety and Professional Services (DSPS)
note: DSPS page opened covers only the dwelling contractor credential (1-2 family homes). Absence of commercial general contractor license rests on secondary sources and DSPS commercial-building pages (plan review). Confirm with DSPS (608-266-2112).

summary: West Virginia requires a state contractor license for commercial work costing $25,000 or more (residential $5,000). Smaller commercial jobs fall below the state requirement.
authority: West Virginia Contractor Licensing Board (Division of Labor)
note: W.Va. Code 30-42-3(d) defines contractor at $5,000 residential / $25,000 commercial; third-party $2,500 figure is outdated. Page lacks the operative mandate section (30-42-5?). Classes include general building and specialty; painting and landscaping excluded; whether partitions-only needs a specialty class is not confirmed. Board FAQ says threshold counts whole project cost, so subs on large jobs may need license.

summary: Wyoming does not license contractors at the state level, except electrical. Licensing is left to the city or county where the work happens, so check local rules.
authority: Wyoming Business Council; local city/county licensing offices
note: Business Council page: 'Contractor licensing (except electrical) is not done by the state of Wyoming...deferred to the local jurisdiction.' Local rules vary (e.g., Cheyenne, Casper not checked).
